content: The shortnose sturgeon, scientifically known as Acipenser brevirostrum, is a relatively small species of sturgeon native to North America. It inhabits 16 to 19 major river and estuary systems along the Atlantic coast, ranging from the Saint John River in New Brunswick, Canada, to the St. Johns River in Florida, United States. The populations of this species are often isolated, as evidenced by the lack of records of individuals in the open sea beyond the influence of their home rivers. Additionally, tagged individuals are rarely captured outside the river systems where they were originally tagged. The species has been found in waters with salinity levels up to 30-31 parts per thousand (ppt), which is slightly less than the salinity of seawater. The shortnose sturgeon is classified as an endangered species in the United States, a designation it has held since 1967. In Canada, it is considered a vulnerable species. This sturgeon is sometimes mistaken for juvenile Atlantic sturgeon because adult shortnose sturgeons are similar in size to the juveniles of the Atlantic species. Before 1973, U.S. commercial fishing records did not distinguish between the two species, and both were collectively referred to as common sturgeon. However, it is believed that most of the catch during that time consisted of Atlantic sturgeon, based on the sizes of the fish recorded. Shortnose sturgeons spawn in freshwater environments, specifically in areas above the tidal influence. They prefer moving water with rubble or gravel bottoms that have minimal silt or organic material. The timing of spawning varies by latitude and is influenced by water temperatures, which typically range from 9 to 12 degrees Celsius, though successful spawning has been observed in temperatures between 6.5 and 15 degrees Celsius. In southern regions such as South Carolina or Georgia, spawning may occur as early as January, while in northern areas like Maine and New Brunswick, it can occur as late as May. Additional spawning requirements include a day length of 13.9 to 14.9 hours and bottom water velocities of 30 to 120 centimeters per second. The eggs of the shortnose sturgeon hatch after approximately 13 days, producing hatchlings that are 7 to 11 millimeters in length. These hatchlings have a large yolk sac, limited vision, minimal swimming ability, and a strong instinct to seek cover. After another 9 to 12 days, they develop into a swimming larval stage, reaching about 15 millimeters in length. By the time they grow to 20 millimeters, they resemble miniature adults and begin feeding. The larvae drift downstream in the deep channels of the river and remain in freshwater for the first year of their lives. Juveniles, which can grow up to 18 inches in length, typically migrate to areas where freshwater and saltwater mix, moving with the tidal cycle. Adult shortnose sturgeons can be found in both freshwater and saltwater environments. They reach sexual maturity at lengths of 45 to 55 centimeters (18 to 22 inches), with the age of maturity varying by latitude. Males in southern rivers, such as those in Georgia, mature after 2 to 3 years, while males in northern rivers, such as those in New Brunswick, take 10 to 14 years to mature. Females mature between 6 and 17 years of age, with earlier maturity occurring in southern populations. Males typically spawn for the first time 1 to 2 years after reaching sexual maturity, while females may take up to 5 additional years before their first spawning event. Adults continue to grow, reaching lengths of 3 to 4 feet. Males may spawn annually or biennially and rarely live beyond 30 years of age. Females, on the other hand, spawn every 3 to 5 years, producing between 40,000 and 200,000 eggs during spawning years. Females can live up to 67 years but experience reduced feeding and growth during the years they are producing gonadal material for reproduction. It is hypothesized, though not definitively proven, that the maximum lifespan of the species is shorter in southern populations and longer in northern populations. In three specific locations—the Connecticut River in Massachusetts, the Santee River in South Carolina, and the Saint John River in New Brunswick—shortnose sturgeons have survived as landlocked populations following the construction of river dams. This demonstrates that the species does not require saltwater to complete its life cycle. Northern populations tend to spend more time in saltwater compared to southern populations, with some northern populations exhibiting an anadromous life cycle (migrating between freshwater and saltwater) rather than an amphidromous one (moving between the two environments without a specific migratory pattern). Shortnose sturgeons are bottom feeders, primarily consuming insects and small crustaceans. Juveniles have been observed with stomach contents containing up to 90% non-food items, suggesting that they may indiscriminately vacuum the riverbed. Adult sturgeons in freshwater primarily feed on mollusks, while their diet in estuarine environments includes polychaetes and small benthic fish. In freshwater, they may also consume crustaceans and insects. The largest known population of shortnose sturgeons is found in the Hudson River, with an estimated 38,000 adults. The second-largest population resides in the Saint John River, with approximately 18,000 adults and a total population of around 100,000 individuals across all age groups. Predation on shortnose sturgeons by non-human species is minimal. Yellow perch have been documented with young sturgeons in their stomachs, and it is believed that sharks and seals may occasionally prey on adult sturgeons. Parasites are not considered harmful to the species, and there are no reported cases of diseases among wild populations. However, one hatchery population has experienced a disease outbreak. Genetically, shortnose sturgeons are 16-ploid, meaning they have chromosomes grouped in sets of 16 rather than the typical paired arrangement found in most vertebrates. It is believed that the shortnose sturgeon may have been one of the most recently evolved sturgeon species.
